There's no doubt about it: The airport lounge wars are heating up with credit card issuers like American Express, Capital One and Chase launching new outposts at a blistering pace.

American Express maintains the largest footprint with its Global Lounge Collection, while Capital One has been expanding its map of Capital One airport lounges.

However, it's Chase in particular that has turned up the heat, expanding its U.S. lounge collection since 2023, with more on the way, including a location at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

Here’s everything you need to know about the family of Chase Sapphire Lounges by The Club, their amenities and how to access them.

Apply for the : Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (see ).

Chase’s lounge collection includes nine Sapphire Lounge locations. The JFK location is temporarily closed.

Additional lounges are planned at the following airports:

Chase has partnered with Airport Dimensions to build out its lounges. Airport Dimensions currently operates dozens of lounges worldwide, most of which are branded as “The Club” or “Club Aspire” and are largely accessible via Priority Pass membership.

Related: Is a Priority Pass lounge membership actually worth it?

This location was the first branded Chase lounge to open in the U.S.

It's located in the Terminal B-to-C connector near gates B39 and B40 and is accessible post-security from Terminals B, C and E. Passengers departing from Terminal A will need to clear security again when returning to their departure terminal.

The lounge has an expansive footprint, at over 11,000 square feet with seating for over 200 guests, though lines to get in can certainly form at busy times, with waits topping an hour. It is open from 5 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

In addition to a variety of restaurant- and living room-style seating areas, there is a self-serve buffet at one end. Guests can also order a la carte dishes created by Boston-area chef Douglass Williams as well as specialty cocktails and Massachusetts-brewed beers from table-mounted QR codes.

The lounge also has wellness rooms with massage chairs and comfortable loungers for relaxation and products from Brooklyn-based fragrance brand Apotheke.

The newest Chase Sapphire Lounge opened at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in July 2026. Located post-security near gate D25 in Terminal D, the 18,000-square-foot lounge is one of the largest in the Sapphire network. It is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

In addition to Chase's signature made-to-order dining (with dishes like blue corn butterscotch pancakes from favorite local restaurant Encina), an all-day buffet and full-service bar, the DFW location introduces several features unique to the network. Travelers can visit the first dedicated Sapphire whiskey lounge featuring guided tastings of Texas whiskeys (and a specialty honey pecan Old Fashioned cocktail), book a complimentary 30-minute Face Haus treatment, freshen up in a shower suite or relax in dedicated rest areas.

Families will also appreciate the children's play area and private nursing room, while travelers in a hurry can take advantage of a grab-and-go food station — a feature Chase is currently testing at this location.

Chase and Airport Dimensions revamped The Etihad Lounge at Dulles, located in Concourse A near gate A14.

The space is small, at just over 5,000 square feet, but features two levels with various seating areas, including a library-themed space, gender-neutral restrooms, shower suites, a reflection room for quiet meditation and a family room.

As with the other lounge locations, this one features locally-inspired food and cocktails plus locally-brewed java from Commonwealth Joe Coffee Roasters.

The lounge is currently open from 6 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily.

Chase's lounge at LAS is located past security in Terminal 1, Concourse C, between gates 23 and 24. It opened in December 2025, spans two stories, covers 4,590 square feet and has seating for up to 87 people. It is open from 4:30 a.m. until 11 p.m. daily.

Though compact compared to the other Chase Sapphire lounges, this one packs a punch in terms of ambience. The space features colorful artwork and a lively atmosphere, not to mention a rather glamorous "Champagne parlor" plus a menu of cocktails inspired by Sin City and a wine list curated by New York retailer Parcelle.

Food options include bites like pork buns and a spicy cucumber salad from Momofuku.

There are no showers, spa services or meditation rooms here, though.

The issuer is bringing a lounge to LAX on an unconfirmed date. It will be adjacent to gate 148 near the connector to the west gates at Tom Bradley International Terminal.

Now that all terminals at LAX are connected airside (post-security), any traveler with access could theoretically visit this lounge, although it is a bit of a hike from other terminals.

The new lounge will measure around 9,000 square feet, which is on the smaller side — especially for an airport the size of LAX — so expect some long wait times once it opens, much as you'll find at the nearby Centurion Lounge.

The Chase Sapphire Lounge by The Club at JFK is located in Terminal 4 near gate A2, not far from the security checkpoint and up one level.

Like the location at IAD, this space is a redesigned Etihad Lounge rather than one Chase created from scratch, and it's rather limited in size at just 7,600 square feet.

It is usually open from 4:30 a.m. until 9 p.m. daily, but at the time of publication, it is temporarily closed due to plumbing issues. There are grab-and-go food options, though.

Typically, you can find a buffet of small plates, plus seasonal items (but always the famous burger) available for order via QR code. This lounge also has three shower suites.

The LaGuardia Sapphire Lounge is the largest of the collection, at 21,000 square feet spanning two floors. It is located in Terminal B and is open from 4:30 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. daily.

The lounge houses plenty of spacious seating areas, including a restaurant-style section and more casual vignettes. There are also family-oriented areas, including a children's playroom and arcade.

The lounge offers a buffet and a seasonal menu featuring select dishes from Sailor, a restaurant in Fort Greene, Brooklyn, plus locally inspired cocktails by Apotheke and wines chosen by Parcelle.

There's also a wellness area where guests can enjoy Face Haus facial treatments, guided meditations from podcaster Devi Brown and private rest pods.

Uniquely, the lounge features Reserve Suites, Chase’s lounge-within-a-lounge concept, which you can reserve for $2,200-$3,000 for a three-hour private retreat.

This 20,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in February 2025 in the connector between Terminal D (home of Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Spirit Airlines, Alaska Airlines and United Airlines) and Terminal E (where gates for Frontier Airlines, JetBlue, Alaska Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Spirit Airlines can be found).

If you go through the Terminal D Transportation Security Administration checkpoint, it is upstairs and is open from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily.

It offers a similar layout to other Chase lounges, but with some unique features including a wellness center with two treatment rooms for facials, two shower suites, a game room, Elixr Coffee drinks and a bar with Philadelphia Eagles-themed cocktails, plus a beer garden and local dishes courtesy of Fishtown eatery Middle Child Clubhouse.

The Sapphire Lounge at PHX opened in November 2024 and is located at the new eight-gate facility in Terminal 4 near gate D11.

This lounge began accepting reservations in June 2025. Sapphire Reserve cardmembers departing from Phoenix can reserve their visit from 14 days up to 24 hours before arriving at the lounge, so you don't have to be physically present to make your reservation. That's because this is the smallest lounge, at just 3,500 square feet.

The lounge is open from 4:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. daily, though its site notes that hours may vary.

There are a few different seating areas, with the tables around the central cocktail bar being in high demand. There's also an indoor terrace separated from the terminal, where a retrofitted Airstream food truck serves specialties from Gallo Blanco. Guests will also find Arizona-based Press Coffee drinks on hand, craft cocktails and a Parcelle-selected list of wines.

Located in San Diego's Terminal 2, this 11,000-square-foot Chase lounge opened in December 2024 with plenty of surfer-themed art and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the tarmac.

The lounge is open from 5 a.m. until 10 p.m. daily and has a swanky wraparound cocktail bar, a small buffet area (plus à la carte dishes by Oscars Mexican Seafood on offer via QR code) and plenty of distinct seating areas.

There's also a wellness area with four relaxation pods and Face Haus treatments, a family room, showers and a nursing room.

Chase is planning a new 16,000-square-foot Sapphire Lounge in Concourse A at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. The Port of Seattle approved the project in October 2026, with a planned $70 million investment covering the initial build-out and a future refurbishment. An opening date has not yet been announced.

Related: 5 ways to ensure you have lounge access before your next flight

Those with the (see rates and fees), (see rates and fees), J.P. Morgan Reserve or Ritz-Carlton™ Credit Card can access these lounges.

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card and the Ritz-Carlton Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Cardholders can access the lounges up to three hours before departure (or up to five hours before a connecting flight) and can also bring up to two guests per visit for free. If you're a cardholder and wish to bring more than two guests, you'll be charged a fee. Children under 2 can enter for free.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve review: A premium card for power travelers

While Priority Pass members previously got to access a Chase Lounge once per calendar year, this benefit has been discontinued.

Select Etihad travelers (the airline’s Gold and Platinum elite members and those flying in business or first class on Etihad-operated flights) can visit the IAD and JFK locations before their flights.

Related: A guide to guest policies for airport lounges

For years, Amex's network of Centurion Lounges was the major player in the card-run lounge space, but in recent years, Chase has quickly caught up, opening a series of lounges around the country in record time, with more on the way. With the airport lounge competition intensifying among major credit card issuers, the real winners are cardholders, though.

That said, these lounges feel like they're getting more crowded by the day, so when you get to an airport with one, make a beeline to the entrance and put your name on the list for access just in case there's a wait. After all, you wouldn't want to miss out on their many amenities.

#6117. Delta Air Lines Vs. United Airlines: Which Carrier’s Boeing 757-300s Are Older?

Boeing 757-300s make up a notable portion of both Delta Air Lines’ and United Airlines’ fleets today. Interestingly, neither ever actively set out to purchase this Boeing narrowbody model — or flying pencil, as it is nicknamed — directly from the manufacturer. Instead, their introduction in each case came about as the by-product of corporate dealings with fellow operators.

Either way, both US legacy carriers have kept 757-300s on their books, taking advantage of the type’s unique blend of size, capacity, and range. Realistically, such characteristics are yet to be matched by any single suitable replacement, meaning both Delta and United have been left with progressively aging flying pencil fleets without an obvious successor. So, with the 757-300 set to remain a feature at both for some time yet, which airlines’ models are older?

Although it is close, United’s 757-300 fleet is older than Delta’s on average. It is also the larger of the two, standing at 21 examples versus Delta’s 16. This places the duo as the two largest operators of the type, after Boeing, which produced only 55 of the models during a relatively short stint between 1998 and 2004. The irony, as mentioned, is that neither United nor Delta actually purchased any variants from Boeing. Rather, each has become the respective largest and second-largest 757-300 operator because of mergers.

In United’s case, the 21 aircraft came under its control following its integration with Continental Airlines, through which their airline operations were unified in 2012. Continental confirmed an order for 15 of the jets in 2001 through a deal estimated at $1.2 billion in list price at the time. Nine of these ultimately made their way to the carrier before it converted the rest of the order to Boeing 737-800s. The remaining 12 were later taken from ATA American Trans Air’s fleet after its collapse in 2009.

Boeing 757-300 specifications, from the manufacturer:

Two Rolls-Royce RB211 / Two Pratt & Whitney PW2000

Similarly, Delta’s 16 757-300s originally flew for Northwest Airlines before the two companies’ operations were integrated in 2010. Northwest initially penned a deal with Boeing in 2001 for 18 of the aircraft, along with two Boeing 747-400s, at a combined list price of $1.75 billion. Following the 9/11 attacks, the order was trimmed to 16. At United, all of the 757-300s Delta received as part of its merger remain in operation today.

Each of United’s 757-300s shares a common internal configuration, housing space for 234 passengers split between two distinct classes. Some 24 United First options make up the front of the cabin. A further 54 United Economy Plus, located primarily directly behind the first class section, alongside 156 United Economy seats fill the remainder of the cabin.

According to the carrier, its first class 757-300 offerings measure 38 inches (96 centimeters) in pitch and 20.4 inches (52 centimeters) in width. United Economy Plus — an extra-legroom economy, rather than a standalone premium product — aboard its 757-300s offers 34-38 inches (86-96 centimeters) of pitch, versus 30-31 inches (76-78 centimeters) in standard United Economy. Each economy option spans up to 17.3 inches (44 centimeters) in width, though the latter can be as narrow as 16.3 inches (41 centimeters).

United Airlines Boeing 757-300 Cabin Specifications, from the airline:

These 757-300s previously had 213 seats onboard — 24 first and 189 economy — before United carried out retrofits from 2018. This came as part of an effort to install slimline seats across its wider fleet, beginning with its Airbus A320 family aircraft in 2012. Under the move, United removed seat-back screens from the Boeing models, instead opting to offer passengers connectivity to its WiFi-enabled personal device inflight entertainment system. All told, the overall offering is not too dissimilar to that on Delta's 757-300s.

Delta and United offer similar experiences on their 757s, except for Delta's long-range 757s in business class.

Each of Delta’s 757-300s also seats 234 passengers, again split between two distinct classes. Similar to United’s models, 24 of these are premium Delta First products. Fewer economy extra — or Delta Comfort in this case — options are available, though, accounting for 38 of the spaces. That leaves additional room for standard Delta Main offerings, which total 172 of the jets’ seats.

As for which airline affords passengers more space on the 757-300, it is a tight contest. Delta First widths of 20.9 inches (53 centimeters) just about trump United’s comparable product, though pitch as low as 37 inches (94 centimeters) can leave marginally more legroom for first-class flyers on the latter. Widths in economy and extra are the same on both, with United Plus potentially offering more pitch than the 33-34 inches (83-86 centimeters) of the Delta Comfort option.

Delta Air Lines Boeing 757-300 Cabin Specifications, from the airline:

Where Delta does arguably have a slight edge is amenities. Alongside onboard WiFi and power outlets, which are both available on United’s 757-300s, Delta’s jets also include seat-back entertainment systems and USB ports, per the carrier. Alongside this, Delta took to refurbishing its 757-300s more recently than United, kicking off interior upgrades in 2024. That is, despite the fleet's relatively old age.

As with any 757-300 flying today, airlines have to keep an eye on aging, given the final model rolled off Boeing’s Renton, Washington, production line back in 2004. This particular model, registered N56859, was originally delivered to Continental and now represents the youngest example among United’s ranks.

Overall, however, United’s 757-300s are slightly older on average than Delta’s. According to data from Ch-aviation, the former’s span is 22.65 to 25.42 years old and averages around 24.3. While that means United has both younger and older specific models than Delta, the latter’s range of 23.15 to 24.77-year-old 757-300s averages approximately 23.8 and is marginally younger in comparison as a whole.

United Airlines and Delta Air Lines’ Boeing 757-300 fleets, from Ch-aviation:

*As of time of writing in late November 2026

Again, it is close, which is somewhat unsurprising given the variant’s production run spanned just six years or so. Either way, with the airframes at each carrier nearing or hovering around the typical lifespan of commercial narrowbodies, one cannot be blamed for wondering about retirement plans. The reality, however, is that neither carrier has yet definitively indicated when this might happen.

Discover the oldest jets in the largest US airline fleets.

So far, only smaller Boeing 757-200s have been dropped by either carrier in efforts to phase out aging 757 family planes. Such variants continue to make up the majority of each fleet for the time being, though both United and Delta were early adopters of the far more popular variant.

Delta received its first in 1984, the year after launch customer Eastern Air Lines debuted the 757-200 commercially. Some 189 models were ultimately operated by Delta over the ensuing years, of which 70 at an average age of 28.4 remain in service, according to Planespotters.net figures. United’s initial 757-200 was delivered not too long after its rival’s in 1988, marking the first of 139 to fly under its colors. Just 40 of these remain today, with these slightly older than Delta’s on the whole, at an average of 29.8 years.

With a longer range of roughly 3,900 nautical miles (7,220 km), the 757-200 was no doubt more successful than its stretched counterpart. Boeing built in excess of 900 airframes designed to typically house 189 passengers, for context. The ever-improving range of newer, similarly sized narrowbodies — like those in the Airbus A321 family — has increasingly offered airlines viable alternatives, nonetheless, opening the door for retirements in turn. Unfortunately for the likes of Delta and United, the same does not go for the specialist, higher-capacity 757-300, which continues to fill a niche.

That has placed the 757-300 in an almost indispensable position, which it still holds today regardless of age. Though Delta and United did not initially swoop in for the variant directly from Boeing, the flying pencil has proven a key tool for serving their high-density domestic routes between hubs, busy leisure destinations, and so on. Not least is its substantial capacity versus rival narrowbodies—a trait that is yet to be replicated by a successor.

For this reason, Delta and United have not just put off retiring the jets, but have actively put resources toward keeping them flying longer. Delta continues to carry out retrofits after kicking off the process in 2024, for instance, while United is poised to overhaul its own 757-300s imminently, according to reports.

#6116. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6115. ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects New Council Members

Edited By: Vanni Gibertini

Last week, ICAO Headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where Member States and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection and sustainable growth.

Over 1,500 delegates from 154 Member States and organizations attended the week-long event thirteen years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

“Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the Conference.

Participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked States, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

The Conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Plan. It also supported liberalizing air services agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since new air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing States. ICAO’s statement continued: “The Conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”

Participants were asked to express their views on the documentation proposing various initiatives with regards to consumer protection legislations that have become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

At the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop Core Principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:

The report for the Seventh Conference invites States to modernize their consumer-protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also says legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries and other providers regarding information, complaints and disruption assistance.

ICAO is expected to review its Core Principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

Many Member States cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

The Conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”

The rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic Member States will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while States will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

During the final two days of the Conference, ICAO held an Extraordinary Session of its Assembly to elect the four additional Council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The Council is the Organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the Assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

Six candidates competed for the four new seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand and Türkiye. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four States won seats.

The Council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the United States and Uruguay.

The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

Few things compare to seeing the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in person on a crisp November morning. Watching massive balloons float down the streets of New York City is an iconic holiday experience on many families’ travel wish lists. Unfortunately, due to severe weather in New York on Nov. 26, 2026, the parade has been postponed to Saturday, Nov. 28.

The last time weather grounded the parade was back in 1971. The parade will now start at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.

Typically, seeing the parade requires forgoing (or delaying) a traditional Thanksgiving meal at home. However, it will likely be well worth the effort once you see your child giddy with excitement as their favorite cartoon characters float by to the tune of a marching band in full regalia, while giant floats with entertainers glide by at street level.

Note, though, that more than 3.5 million people attend the parade in person each year. It’s important to strategize your visit so you are not far from the curb, struggling to catch a glimpse of the street.

There are several things you’ll want to keep in mind as you plan your day at the parade. Here are our top tips for viewing the 100th annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026.

If you want to get an up-close view of the balloons featured in the annual parade, you won’t want to miss the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Balloon Inflation. Inflation occurs the day before the parade, starting at 1 p.m. on the Upper West Side, at 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, near the American Museum of Natural History. It runs until 6 p.m., so you have several hours to sneak a peek at what’s to come during the parade. (Tip: The line opens at noon.)

There are 32 balloons that will transform from flat to fully inflated during the course of the afternoon. There are some fun new floats to keep an eye out for this year. To name a few, Bob the Minion riding a giant banana, Sorcerer Mickey, the Geico gecko and Earl the Squirrel, a balloon based on a real-life squirrel who made his home in Universal Orlando's Christmas tree several years ago and has now become the park's official holiday mascot.

Inflating a giant balloon the height of a four-story building takes time. Long lines form as the balloons become fully inflated in the early evening, so you may want to test your luck by arriving closer to 3 p.m., when most of the balloons start taking shape.

To get to the event location via public transportation, allow extra time; the subway station at 72nd Street tends to get very crowded as the afternoon wears on. You can also hail a cab or use a ride-hailing service, though you’ll want to be dropped off a block or two north of the gated-off section to avoid delays. Once you're in the line, you'll progress north and can exit west along any block from West 82nd to West 86th streets.

TPG tip: The closest subway station to the entrance point is the B and C stop at 72nd Street and Central Park West. Consider taking the 1, 2 or 3 train to Broadway and 72nd Street instead. It’s a few blocks west but an easy walk — just follow the crowds.

Related: These are the best New York City hotels for families to check out

Some parade-goers arrive as early as 4 a.m. to snag a coveted front-row spot along the route.

Plan accordingly if you have a particular location in mind. For example, prime seats at covered bus stops start filling up around 4 a.m., while you might be able to get front-row curb seating closer to 6 a.m.

Should you have deeper pockets and want to avoid being outside in the elements, you can pay for a parade brunch with a view along the parade route. Just be sure to make these reservations well in advance, as they tend to fill up quickly. Or, of course, you could book a room with a view directly on the parade route.

For those arriving later in the morning, you can stand in the closed-off side streets leading to the parade. You might be 10-15 people back, but you can still see most of the action.

The parade starts at 8:30 a.m. at Central Park West on 77th Street. Since the route is 2.5 miles long, it can take close to an hour for the lead marchers to reach Macy's. This means you’ll have some idle time before you can start watching the spectacle.

Because you could find yourself waiting several hours for the parade to show up, you’ll want to bring some stuff to stay occupied, like snacks, drinks and games. A backup charger is also a good idea.

You can bring camping chairs, buckets or anything else you may want to sit on to the parade, though these items are not very helpful for the parade itself, since most people stand. Still, at the very least, you’ll probably want to have some hotel towels or blankets to sit on instead of the hard, cold, gum-covered New York City sidewalks.

Don’t forget proper attire, including jackets, hats, gloves and umbrellas if rain is in the forecast, since the weather can turn quickly in late fall.

Like at home, excitement builds as the parade start time nears, and before long, cheers erupt as the parade comes into view. However, what you may not realize from watching at home is how interactive the experience can be. You may get high-fives from clowns and even confetti in your hair.

Not everything you see on TV happens along the parade route, either. Some performances, including those by the Radio City Rockettes and various singing and dance groups, only occur in front of Macy’s Herald Square (where the cameras are). As a result, you’ll want to manage your expectations. Don’t worry about what you’re missing. Instead, focus on all that’s taking place in front of you: the floats, balloons and festivities.

Related: 10 tips for flying during the holidays

The parade covers so much of the city that there isn’t one best hotel for attending the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. While some hotels are physically on the parade route, it’s not as simple as booking a room at one of these properties and watching the festivities from your window.

Sure, some windows at the route-adjacent hotels offer good views — but hotels are savvy, so those rooms are often sold as part of pricier parade packages. As such, you’ll have to pay more and often meet minimum stay requirements to see the parade from your actual hotel room.

If you don’t want to splurge to see all the action from your room, ask if your hotel has a special viewing area for guests. Often, hotels on the parade route have some space outside where patrons can watch the parade as it passes.

A few properties on the parade route include:

Should you have trouble securing a room at a property on the parade route or wish to save a little money, consider staying a block or more off the route at properties like The St. Regis New York and Park Hyatt New York. Both are a very short walk to and from the parade.

Some more points-friendly hotels that are within walking distance of the parade route include:

Related: 10 festive hotels for people who really love the holidays

Since New York City is an incredible place to be for the holidays, there are all kinds of other ways to celebrate the season after kicking it off with the parade. Be sure to see Santa in person at Santaland on the eighth floor of Macy’s on 34th Street (reservations are required). The Big Apple Circus, under the big top in Lincoln Center, is a sure-fire family pleaser. Also, peruse some of the festive holiday markets throughout the city when you’re not busy ice skating at Rockefeller Center or catching a performance of a Christmas classic like “The Nutcracker” or “A Christmas Carol.”

#6111. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6110. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#6109. Only 22% Full: Breeze Airways' 11 Emptiest Routes Revealed

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Utah-based Breeze Airways has carved out a niche for nonstop flights in secondary markets across the US. The low-cost carrier offers a unique point-to-point market on underserved domestic routes and operates a fleet of modern Airbus A220-300s.

Reviewing data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) suggests that a number of its routes are flying below the 'sweet spot' of 80% load factor. This is a target most airlines set to ensure that all operational costs are covered and that the route turns a profit. Overall, the average Breeze load factor sits at 77.9%.

Despite Breeze's rapid expansion across the US since the airline's launch in 2021, the airline's primary focus has been connecting secondary cities with nonstop flights. Reviewing the data from BTS, it suggests the airline's poorest performing routes flew with an average of less than 46% during the period of January to August 2026.

These low numbers are the polar opposite to the airline's fullest routes, which average more than 91% load factor, with the most popular route for the airline being that of Atlantic City (ACY) to Orlando (MCO), achieving a 93.8% average load factor.

As a comparison, the poorest performing route was between Orange County (SNA) and Montrose (MTJ), which averaged load factors of just 22.4%, which forced the carrier to suspend the service in April of this year.

Average Load Factor (Between January and August 2026)

With Orange County and Montrose having the poorest load factors, which led to the route being suspended, a number of other routes in the Breeze network are still performing with low patronage, questioning whether the airline may reconsider these routes. Simple Flying reached out to Breeze for comment on the below routes' load factors; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

For Breeze, its second-worst-performing route is between Charleston (CHS) in South Carolina and Richmond (RIC) in Virginia. The route continues to operate, despite a load factor averaging 38.5%. This is followed by Louisville (SDF) and Pittsburgh (PIT), which began in April and have only been able to achieve a 42.8% load factor. This route is expected to end in January.

Flights from Washington Dulles (IAD) nonstop to Ogdensburg (OGS) in upstate New York are another route that was forced to end due to load factors, with Breeze operating at just 45.6%. Full details of the airline's poorest-performing routes are in the table below:

Began in January, seasonal pause from September to December)

Airlines will typically aim for an 80% passenger load factor, to cover high fixed costs and historically thin profit margins. Aiming for 80% helps cover the operating costs and turns the flight profitable. This can fluctuate between airlines, but this is the industry benchmark.

Underused seasonal links have crumbled under poor loads while the airline pivots its fleet toward bigger Myrtle Beach plans.

After Atlantic City to Orlando remains the airline's most popular route by load factor, the carrier's transcontinental services continue to pull high patronage. The airline's second most popular route is that of Norfolk (ORF) to San Diego (SAN), which during the period of January to August of this year recorded a 93% load factor.

Los Angeles (LAX) to Richmond is another popular link, which during the same period achieved 92.3% load factor. Los Angeles to Norfolk followed with 92.2%, and Los Angeles to Jacksonville (JAX) reached 91.7%. Full details below, excluding Atlantic City to Orlando as already outlined in the first table.

#6108. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

#6106. Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

This was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:

The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:

Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM

The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was launched in the first place, and is sticking around.

While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

#6105. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#6104. Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card

Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

The card also has no extra cost to add authorized users, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:

Personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

Southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

Preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

If you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:

The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:

I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

If you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

If you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.
