#6103. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

Love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

That said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

After a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself…

Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

Getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

The screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

Ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

#6102. Why American Airlines’ Late Bet On The Airbus A319 Is Still Paying Off

American Airlines has built one of the world's largest Airbus A319 fleets, despite initially arriving relatively late to the aircraft compared with several other major operators. What might once have appeared to be a relatively modest addition to its narrowbody lineup has developed into an important part of the airline's short-haul operation, providing the capacity, flexibility, and operating economics needed across hundreds of short-haul routes.

Today, American Airlines operates 133 examples of the Airbus A319, making it the world's largest operator of the type. Although many of these aircraft are approaching or have passed two decades in service, their comparatively low ownership costs, established maintenance infrastructure, and suitability for demanding domestic markets have helped extend their usefulness. Rather than rushing to retire the fleet, American Airlines is increasingly demonstrating why its decision to embrace the smaller Airbus narrowbody continues to make financial and operational sense.

American Airlines did not originally develop its Airbus A319 fleet through a single, coordinated purchasing program. Instead, its current position resulted from several acquisitions, corporate mergers, and opportunities to obtain secondhand aircraft at attractive prices. The most significant contribution came from its 2013 merger with US Airways, which brought a substantial number of established A319s into the combined airline's operations and immediately increased its exposure to the type.

US Airways was one of the original customers for the Airbus A319, having recognized the aircraft's potential for operating routes where larger narrowbodies would offer more capacity than necessary. Through the merger, American Airlines inherited 66 A319s, giving it a considerable foundation on which to build. The combined airline subsequently supplemented this inherited fleet with additional aircraft, eventually establishing a presence that few other operators could match.

American Airlines also ordered 32 brand-new A319s, which were delivered between 2013 and 2015. These aircraft are considerably younger than most of the examples inherited from US Airways and represent a particularly distinctive part of the fleet. They are also the only A319s currently operating with a US airline to feature Airbus' fuel-saving sharklets, making them visually and technically different from the airline's older examples.

The remaining aircraft came through various fleet transitions involving US Airways, America West Airlines, and Frontier Airlines, including secondhand additions as other operators reduced their Airbus A319 commitments. This mixed acquisition strategy has allowed American Airlines to expand without relying entirely on expensive new deliveries. Consequently, its fleet now combines relatively young aircraft with older examples that have already delivered substantial value to their previous owners.

The strongest argument for retaining the Airbus A319 is its relatively inexpensive ownership cost, particularly when compared with purchasing or leasing a substantially newer aircraft. American Airlines already has the infrastructure, maintenance expertise, pilot training arrangements, and operational experience required to support the type. Adding another used A319 therefore involves fewer complications than introducing an entirely different aircraft family into its existing narrowbody operation.

American Airlines has previously described being the world's largest A319 operator as "one of our hidden advantages", explaining that acquiring additional examples of a type already present in such significant numbers can be very cost-effective. This advantage becomes particularly important when aircraft become available on the secondhand market, allowing the airline to expand capacity without accepting the financial commitments associated with purchasing brand-new aircraft.

The changing aircraft market has also created favorable conditions for American Airlines. As more Airbus A220 aircraft enter service with airlines around the world, older A319s are increasingly becoming available, particularly as aircraft complete their initial leasing arrangements. For an operator that already understands the type and has the necessary maintenance arrangements in place, these opportunities can provide an economical way to secure additional capacity.

There is, of course, a difference between acquiring an inexpensive aircraft and operating one profitably. Maintenance requirements, fuel consumption, reliability, and the cost of keeping older interiors competitive all influence the overall economics. Nevertheless, American Airlines benefits from having an established fleet large enough to spread many of these expenses across numerous aircraft. This makes the A319 considerably more attractive than it might be to a smaller operator.

The latest data from ch-aviation shows that American Airlines currently operates the following Airbus A320 family aircraft:

The two carriers are among the largest in the world when measured by fleet size.

The Airbus A319's relatively modest capacity is particularly useful across American Airlines' extensive domestic network, where passenger demand can vary considerably between individual routes. While larger narrowbodies are essential for high-volume services, deploying them everywhere would not necessarily make economic sense. The A319 provides an alternative, allowing the airline to maintain frequencies and serve important markets without consistently offering more seats than passengers require.

American Airlines deploys its fleet of Airbus A319s on a wide variety of routes, with the aircraft providing flexibility when capacity needs to be matched with local demand and available airport infrastructure. One common route for the aircraft is between Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

This is an especially interesting example because both airports present operational challenges, including significant congestion and restrictions on available slots. Smaller aircraft can be particularly useful in such circumstances, allowing American Airlines to serve important business markets while managing capacity within the limitations of busy airports.

The Airbus A319 also provides useful flexibility when passenger numbers change throughout the year or when an airline needs to adjust its schedules. Rather than reducing frequencies or abandoning a market, American Airlines can deploy a smaller aircraft while continuing to offer convenient departure times. This makes the type valuable not simply because it is inexpensive, but because its capacity matches the commercial requirements of numerous individual routes.

American Airlines' position is particularly interesting when considered against the history of the Airbus A319 in the US. Other airlines had already established themselves as important operators before American Airlines consolidated its fleet through the US Airways merger. However, entering the market later did not necessarily put American Airlines at a disadvantage, because it inherited an established operation rather than having to develop an entirely new one from scratch.

The airline also benefited from the opportunity to acquire aircraft at different stages of their operating lives. Its 32 factory-delivered A319s arrived between 2013 and 2015, while many of its other examples were already established aircraft with considerable service histories. This combination provides a mixture of newer and older airframes, giving American Airlines different options when allocating aircraft to routes and planning maintenance.

Another advantage comes from the relative simplicity of maintaining a fleet built around a familiar aircraft family. Although the A319 is not identical to the A320 or A321, the shared Airbus narrowbody heritage creates operational commonality that can help airlines manage training, maintenance, and fleet planning. American Airlines can therefore benefit from its existing Airbus expertise while continuing to operate aircraft with different seating capacities.

The wider aviation industry is also experiencing renewed interest in smaller narrowbody aircraft, although newer designs are pursuing similar markets with different technologies. The COMAC C919 illustrates how manufacturers are seeking to challenge established aircraft families, but neither changes the immediate economic appeal of an existing A319 fleet with established support arrangements. For American Airlines, proven aircraft and favorable acquisition costs remain compelling considerations.

The Boeing 737-700 and Airbus A319 are renowned for their unique capabilities, but which is actually cheaper to fly?

Perhaps the clearest indication of how much American Airlines values its A319 fleet is the changing retirement schedule. The oneworld carrier was at one point expected to begin retiring its approximately 100 older examples as early as 2026. However, American Airlines has since pushed the expected retirement timeline back to at least 2030, suggesting that the aircraft remain commercially useful beyond their originally anticipated operating lives.

Extending the retirement date does not mean that the airline intends to operate its aircraft indefinitely. Older narrowbodies inevitably become more expensive to maintain as components age, and the financial benefits of keeping them eventually diminish. Nevertheless, when replacement aircraft are expensive, delivery positions are limited, and demand remains strong, extending the service life of existing aircraft can be a sensible way to protect capacity.

American Airlines is also investing in its Airbus A319 interiors rather than simply allowing the cabins to deteriorate. The refurbishment program brings the aircraft closer to the airline's newer interior standards and includes an additional row of first-class seating. This is an important commercial consideration because it allows the airline to generate more premium-cabin revenue without acquiring a larger aircraft or substantially changing its existing route structure.

The interior changes have not been universally welcomed by passengers, particularly following the removal of seatback entertainment screens from some refurbished aircraft. However, American Airlines has indicated that it intends to bring seatback screens back to its narrowbody fleet from 2028. This suggests that its cabin strategy is still evolving, with the airline balancing refurbishment costs, passenger expectations, and the financial benefits of retaining aircraft that would otherwise require replacement.

American Airlines' continued investment in the A319 also needs to be understood within the context of its wider fleet modernization program. The airline operates several narrowbody types, each serving different requirements across its domestic and international networks. Newer aircraft provide improvements in fuel efficiency, passenger experience, and maintenance performance, but replacing every older aircraft immediately would create significant financial pressure and operational challenges.

The Airbus A319 offers an effective bridge between the airline's established fleet and its newer aircraft deliveries. Its smaller capacity is particularly useful in markets where demand does not justify deploying an Airbus A321, while its existing operating infrastructure reduces the costs associated with keeping it in service. This allows American Airlines to concentrate investment on areas where new aircraft can deliver the greatest benefits rather than replacing every older airframe simply because of its age. There is also an important distinction between the economics of operating a used aircraft and those of purchasing a new one. A brand-new narrowbody may offer better fuel efficiency, but its acquisition cost, financing commitments, and depreciation must all be considered. An older Airbus A319 that has already been acquired at a relatively low price can remain competitive on routes where its operating costs are manageable, and passenger demand supports its capacity.

Ultimately, American Airlines' relationship with the A319 demonstrates how a fleet strategy does not always need to revolve around the newest aircraft to deliver meaningful commercial advantages. Its late expansion into the type, supported by the US Airways merger and subsequent secondhand acquisitions, has created a substantial fleet that continues to serve hundreds of routes.

With retirements postponed, interiors receiving attention, and used aircraft remaining comparatively affordable, the Airbus A319 appears likely to remain an important part of American Airlines' domestic operation for several more years.

#6101. New FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some new restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a new rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”

The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

Given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:

The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major issues, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”

A new FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy

While the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉

As of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

What do you make of the FAA’s new restrictions on takeoff?

ALL Accor reward points have a fixed value when you redeem them toward eligible hotel stays: 1,000 points get you 20 euros off. That gives each reward point a hotel stay value of 2 euro cents and is why TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Accor points at 2.25 cents.

ALL Accor reward points expire after 365 consecutive days without eligible point-earning activity. Any qualifying activity that credits at least one reward point extends the validity of your entire balance for another 365 days. An eligible donation of reward points can also extend the validity of your balance.

ALL Accor doesn't price hotel awards as traditional free nights. Instead, you can generally redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay. When redeeming online, you can use 1,000 points for 20 euros off or 2,000 points for 40 euros off; after that, redemption amounts generally increase in increments of 2,000 points.

You can earn ALL Accor Silver, Gold or Platinum status through either status nights or status points within a calendar year. Silver requires 10 nights or 2,000 status points, Gold requires 30 nights or 7,000 status points, and Platinum requires 60 nights or 14,000 status points. Diamond status requires 26,000 status points and can't be earned through nights alone, while Limitless status is available by invitation only.

An eligible stay paid for in part or in full with reward points can still earn status nights. However, you'll only earn reward points and status points on the eligible portion of the bill that you pay without reward points.

The ALL Accor loyalty program works differently from many hotel programs familiar to U.S. travelers. Reward points have a fixed value in euros toward most eligible hotel stays, elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, and paid memberships can help you save on stays and accelerate your progress toward status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming ALL Accor points, qualifying for elite status and deciding whether the program is a good fit for you.

ALL Accor is the hotel loyalty program for Accor Group. The program covers over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands in 110-plus countries worldwide, ranging from Fairmont and Pullman to Mercure and Ibis.

Accor has an especially strong footprint in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. Its comparatively limited North American footprint makes ALL Accor less appealing to many U.S.-based travelers.

You can become a member of ALL Accor by visiting the program's website and clicking the sign-up button in the upper-right corner. From there, it's a quick and easy process to sign up for the free-to-join ALL Accor program.

You'll see two different points balances in your ALL Accor account: reward points and status points. Reward points are what you can redeem for stays and other rewards, while status points are one of the ways you can earn ALL Accor status.

When you book an eligible stay — which generally excludes stays booked through online travel agencies — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, as well as status points based on the brand and your eligible pretax spending.

Specifically, here's how many reward points and status points you'll earn per 10 euros (about $11) spent:

So, a Classic member staying at an Adagio Access property would earn 500 reward points and 500 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending, while a Diamond elite member would earn double the reward points but the same number of status points. Meanwhile, 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending at a Fairmont would earn 2,500 status points regardless of elite tier, but a Classic member would earn 2,500 reward points while a Diamond elite member would earn 5,000 reward points.

Accor has more than 45 brands; here's an overview of the Accor Group brands:

However, not all of these brands participate fully in ALL Accor. The list of excluded hotels and brands is rather long, but note that no HotelF1 properties participate, most Ibis Budget properties are excluded and only select The Hoxton hotels participate.

ALL Accor also includes select third-party “Partner of ALL Accor” properties. Earning and elite benefits may vary at these hotels, and reward points can't be used to reduce the cost of stays at IntercityHotel, Steigenberger, Steigenberger Icon, Maxx, Jaz in the City or Zleep properties.

The ALL Accor hotel loyalty program has an entry tier, four earnable elite status tiers and an invitation-only Limitless tier. Members can also benefit from select paid memberships and occasional status match or challenge opportunities.

Status nights and status points reset at the start of each calendar year. Once you reach a new tier, you'll keep it for the rest of that calendar year and the following calendar year. To retain it beyond then, you must requalify during the next calendar year.

ALL Accor members have Classic status if they don't qualify for elite status. So, as soon as you join ALL Accor, you'll enjoy Classic benefits, including:

You can earn ALL Accor Silver status when you stay 10 nights or earn 2,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Classic members, Silver elite members get the following perks:

If you happen to have Gold status with Qatar Airways Privilege Club, you can link your account with ALL Accor and upgrade to Silver status after your first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Gold status when you stay 30 nights or earn 7,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Silver elite members, Gold elite members get the following perks:

Some cards issued outside the U.S. offer ALL Accor Gold status as a cardmember perk, though none issued in the U.S. currently do. And Qatar Airways Privilege Club Platinum members can upgrade to ALL Accor Gold status after their first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Platinum status when you stay 60 nights or earn 14,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Gold elite members, Platinum elite members get the following perks:

Once you reach 60 nights or 14,000 status points within a calendar year, you'll earn two suite night upgrades. Each suite night upgrade guarantees a one-night upgrade to a suite. You can earn an additional suite night upgrade for every additional 4,000 status points you earn.

You can earn ALL Accor Diamond status when you accrue at least 26,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Platinum elite members, Diamond elite members get the following perks:

ALL Accor also has an invitation-only Limitless status, which Accor grants at its discretion. In addition to all the Diamond benefits, Limitless members get 24-hour access to a personal assistant and concierge service, can gift Platinum status to a person of their choice and can transfer reward points to as many as five other ALL Accor members (up to 12 transfers per year).

ALL Accor offers three paid ALL Accor+ memberships: ALL Accor+ Explorer, ALL Accor+ Voyager and ALL Accor+ Ibis.

These subscriptions offer discounts, a boost toward higher elite status and various other perks. Although ALL Accor+ subscriptions can be combined, ALL Accor caps the bonus status nights you can receive from subscription programs and cobranded cards at 30 per account, per calendar year.

I've considered buying the ALL Accor+ Ibis membership, as its 15% discount could cover the 99-euro annual fee once you spend about 660 euros on eligible stays booked at the subscription rate.

You have many opportunities to earn reward points and status points with Accor. Here's an overview of the options most relevant for U.S. residents.

When you book an eligible stay — which excludes stays booked through online travel websites — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, plus status points based on the brand and the cost of your stay. Specifically, Classic members earn reward points and status points as follows:

Elite members earn additional reward points on top of what Classic members earn; Silver members get 24% additional reward points, Gold members get 48% additional reward points, Platinum members get 76% additional reward points, and Diamond and Limitless members get 100% additional reward points. However, elite members don't earn any additional status points over what Classic members earn.

So, while a Classic member would earn 1,250 reward points and 1,250 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending on an Ibis stay, a Platinum member would earn 2,200 reward points and 1,250 status points on the same stay.

You'll earn reward points and status points not just for your room but also for meals, minibar, spa and other eligible charges to your room. Plus, if you opt to Skip the Clean, you'll earn 100 reward points per day skipped. And keep in mind that you can earn reward points — but not status points or nights — on day rooms at participating Accor properties.

You can earn reward points on rental cars from three partners as follows:

You can earn reward points by clicking through the Collections site before shopping.

You can earn up to 600 reward points on your first survey with Club Opinions. And with e-Rewards, you can earn 250 reward points on your first survey.

You can convert the following transferable rewards into ALL Accor reward points as follows:

Transfers are final, though, so make sure converting your rewards to ALL Accor is the best-value option before you transfer.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

You can earn reward points as follows when you convert select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards:

After linking your ALL Accor account with an eligible airline loyalty account, you may be able to earn reward points on select flights in addition to the rewards you earn with the airline program. For example, you can earn 1 reward point per $2 spent on eligible Qatar Airways flights and 1 reward point per 2 euros spent on eligible Air France-KLM flights.

Elite members with Gold status or higher in ALL Accor or Qantas Frequent Flyer can earn 1 reward point per 4 Australian dollars (about $3) spent on eligible Qantas flights, while ALL Accor members with Silver status or higher and Azul Fidelidade members with Diamante status can earn 1 reward point for every 7.50 euros spent on eligible Azul flights.

You can earn 1 reward point and 1 status point per 2 euros spent when you host a group of at least eight attendees (or at least eight rooms) at a participating hotel. It doesn't matter whether your event is a professional gathering or personal celebration.

You have plenty of options for redeeming Accor points. As with earning, we'll focus on redemptions most relevant to U.S. residents.

ALL Accor lets you redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay at a participating hotel. You can use points toward part or, in some cases, all of your stay, although some prepaid rates require a portion to be paid by card.

To redeem points for a hotel stay online, log in to your ALL Accor account and search for a stay as normal. When you choose a rate at a specific hotel, look for one with a purple "Pay with your points" designation if you want to redeem points for part or all of your stay.

Near the end of the booking process, you can opt to redeem points toward your stay. For example, I could redeem 1,000 points for 20 euros off my stay and pay the remaining balance with a credit card.

These hotel stay redemptions provide a fixed value of 2 euro cents per point, so you generally won't get outsize value from your reward points.

You can redeem — and, in some cases, bid — Accor points for select entertainment, dining and sports experiences through the ALL Limitless Experiences page. There are some great deals to be found, too, such as this Christmas Eve dinner for just 600 points.

You can also redeem Accor points for select activities through ALL Accor Activities & Events.

It's worth checking both of these programs periodically to see whether any experiences fit your upcoming schedule and tastes.

You can redeem your Accor reward points for select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards as follows:

I don't usually recommend transferring hotel points to other travel loyalty programs, as you'll typically lose a good bit of value. Check TPG's valuations and calculate your redemption rate before transferring ALL Accor points to another program.

ALL Accor is most compelling for travelers who frequently visit Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region, where Accor has a much larger footprint than in North America. Its hotel redemptions are also easy to understand: 1,000 reward points generally get you 20 euros off an eligible stay.

However, that simplicity means you generally won't find the outsize hotel redemptions that are possible with programs that use award charts or dynamic pricing. ALL Accor also lacks a U.S.-issued cobranded credit card, and its U.S.-accessible transfer partners generally transfer at less than a 1:1 ratio.

Elite status can still be useful, especially at the Platinum and Diamond levels, which offer perks such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions or on certain days. Finally, ALL Accor+ subscriptions may be useful for some travelers.

ALL Accor probably won't be the best primary hotel program for most U.S.-based travelers given its relatively limited North American footprint, lack of a U.S.-issued cobranded card and less-than-1:1 transfer ratios. But it may be useful if you frequently stay at Accor brands in Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region.

Reward points are easy to use at a fixed value toward eligible hotel stays, while higher elite tiers offer potentially valuable benefits such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast. Frequent Accor guests should consider whether an ALL Accor+ subscription could pay for itself through discounts, status nights and other benefits.

Even if you don't plan to pursue status, it's worth joining ALL Accor before your next eligible stay to access member rates and earn reward points.

#6099. BermudAir Adding Flights All Over The Place: I Don’t Know What’s Going On

BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

For a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

Several months back, BermudAir announced new winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:

On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:

Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed…

I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:

I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:

What’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know…

It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”

What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

#6098. LATAM Refused My Refund Within 24 Hours, And The Reason Makes No Sense

Over the weekend, I booked an expensive ticket for my dad, brother, and me, from Buenos Aires (EZE) to Santiago (SCL), only to come across a better deal after I’d booked. I called customer service to cancel within the 24-hour cooling-off period, but was refused a refund for the most convoluted and unnecessary reason.

LATAM is the airline I’ve flown with the second most in my life after British Airways, my old home airline. It’s an airline I look forward to flying with for several reasons. However, this recent booking experience has uncovered a gaping hole in its customer service, which in the air I’ve always found to be excellent.

This whole situation could have been avoided if I’d been able to pay with my UK credit card on LATAM’s Brazilian website.

The Brazilian site has no issue when entering UK credit card details.

However, the default setting for postcodes (ZIP codes) is numerical-only because, as in the US, Brazil’s postcodes consist only of numbers. In the UK, they’re made up of letters and numbers, so I couldn’t add the postcode that my credit card is registered to.

I tried using only the numbers of my postcode (the one in the example above is random), but the site returned an error, saying it failed to connect to my bank. My guess would be this wouldn’t be a problem for US credit cards, given that ZIP codes consist only of numbers too.

I remember this happening previously, but I never had an issue with a booking that I couldn’t change online.

Ideally, I would have paid with a Brazilian bank account or credit card, but I’m still working through the immigration bureaucracy required to open one.

First of all, I tried to cancel by logging into my LATAM Pass account, but was redirected to the contact center. This is when I realized how much of an obstacle my booking via the UK website would be.

After being put on hold 3 times for what seemed like forever, the agent I spoke with at LATAM’s Brazilian call center told me there was nothing she could do to help me.

She explained the only way I’d get a refund was to call the UK call center, since I’d paid in GBP on the UK website. I called just before the cut-off of the 24-hour cooling-off period, so by then I had exceeded it. I had only left it so close to the cooling-off period because I was researching the trip again the following day and found a better deal; otherwise, I wouldn’t have wanted to cancel.

If I had called sooner and had more time, I could have asked someone in the UK to call for me, as my Brazilian phone number can’t make outgoing international calls. I did top up my UK SIM Card with 20 GBP, but at a charge of 2 GBP per minute, the call disconnected after 10 minutes on hold with no answer.

Irrespective of whether I could have found an easier way to contact the UK call center, I can’t help but feel that my issue should have been resolved there and then over the phone by the Brazilian call center agent. After all, I booked directly through the airline’s website, and then called the airline directly to cancel. It makes no logical sense!

Because of a stupidly convoluted system, I’m stuck with a LATAM ticket that I can no longer cancel, even though I called customer service within the 24-hour cooling-off period.

It’s not the end of the world, as we can still take the flights we’d originally booked, but it’s so frustrating to be put in a situation like this in 2026 because of such an archaic technicality.

I’m still a big fan of LATAM itself, and will continue to fly it, at least until my Platinum status runs out next year.

What’s the most frustrating post-sale customer service experience you’ve had?

#6097. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”
