‘The Five’ weighs in on Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia following an affair scandal and his admission to additional affairs. The panel examines Democrats’ response, his welcome back to the company and questions about potential national security implications.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance helped bring Jensen Huang back to the helm of Nvidia — a move that has reportedly exposed divisions within the administration and prompted one expert to warn it is "sending the wrong message."

The push to get Huang his job back has reportedly put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the handling of national-security concerns involving Huang’s relationship with a woman whose alleged ties to Chinese intelligence remain in dispute, as well as questions about advanced U.S. chips reaching China.

Vance reportedly worked with Nvidia's board over the weekend to get Huang his job back, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who reportedly warned Trump about intelligence concerning the relationship, took another approach. Rubio has not publicly weighed in on the CEO's reinstatement and his office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The Vice President told CNN on Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche assured him that Huang was not under investigation.

"But most importantly, at just, I think, a personal level, we received the assurances that he was not under any significant, he was under no investigation, and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," he said.

Vance continued, saying that he didn't think it was appropriate anyone should lose their job "because anonymous sources accuse them of things in the New York Times."

The Nvidia saga reveals a "definitively split approach within the administration" toward China, as the company pressed for looser export controls, Max Meizlish of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies told Fox News Digital.

President Donald Trump, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent, left, and Secretary of Commerce nominee Howard Lutnick, speaks to the press as he signs an executive order to create a US sovereign wealth fund, in the Oval Office of the White House on February 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. TRUMP DEFENDS JENSEN HUANG'S CREDIBILITY, NVIDIA'S FUTURE AFTER BOARD REINSTATED CEO, SAYS 'SEX SELLS'

Nvidia said it received assurances from senior officials that Huang's reinstatement posed no national-security risk. But federal investigations were still underway into the Nvidia CEO's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential diversion of advanced U.S. chips to China when the president began his push.

The decision to reinstate Huang has left Republican lawmakers demanding to know what senior administration officials told Nvidia’s board that led them to reverse course less than two weeks after Huang's resignation.

The scrutiny intensified Monday when the Commerce Department added Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company tied to Huang’s former affair partner, to its trade blacklist after months of reported disagreement inside the administration over restricting the firm under investigation for allegedly helping divert Nvidia chips to the CCP.

Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Jay Clayton, however, said Sunday that investigations into Megaspeed and executive Alice Huang were ongoing, urging officials to "let that investigation play out" and "gather the facts."

Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the U.S. government had no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China, making the company’s technology a focal point in the U.S.-China race for AI leadership. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

But when asked Monday night whether Huang had been cleared of national-security concerns or violations of federal law, Blanche declined to say. Meizlish questioned the administration’s commitment to preventing chip diversion and told Fox News Digital that restoring Huang "is clearly sending the wrong message."

Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, is under scrutiny over alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed is being investigated over possible diversion of advanced chips to China.

Bessent said Nov. 13 that Treasury, the State Department, the Pentagon and the U.S. Trade Representative had "for months" supported adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, but conceded that "Commerce has the pen" to decide whether to take action.

Bessent said his deputy had been pushing for action. Prior reporting indicates Commerce officials resisted the move while other administration officials pressed for restrictions. Trump later acknowledged that Lutnick may have delayed action to avoid a "blowup with China."

President Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio look on during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Republican lawmakers are pressing for answers about what the administration knew before Nvidia’s board decided to bring Huang back.

Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., called Huang’s reinstatement a "mistake," warning it could "whitewash" unresolved national-security questions.

The Republican chairmen of the House committees on Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China said the board’s "brief internal investigation and reinstatement" did not erase the threats and questions they are investigating. The congressional scrutiny comes amid separate questions about why it took months to blacklist Megaspeed and whether the controls now in place go far enough.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

Commerce added Megaspeed and six affiliates to the Entity List Monday, the same day Nvidia announced Huang’s return. The designation requires licenses for covered exports to the companies, with applications subject to a presumption of denial.

"Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings," the department said. It explained the listing makes it unlawful to export U.S.-origin goods, software or technology to Megaspeed, and that advanced SI chips are also barred even when made overseas.

Applying the entity-specific FDPR, he said, could further restrict the company’s access to foreign-made chips and components. Commerce did not specify whether H20 chips or the other components McGuire cited are covered by the existing rules.

The White House maintains that its policy has been consistent, with spokesman Matthew Middleton telling Fox News Digital that "America’s most advanced chips must go to U.S. SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies."

A White House official also said Trump has repeatedly ruled out allowing China to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell and Rubin chips, and noted that Megaspeed has been under federal investigation since 2024 and Nvidia placed the company on its internal "no sell" list in June 2025.

Commerce said last week that the DOJ later took the lead in the criminal investigation. Neither department has announced charges against Megaspeed.

#6042. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

#6041. Why deep pockets weren’t enough to save the GOP in 2026: 'Money is not magic'

Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.

Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE

GOP electoral efforts were buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC. (Getty Images)

On top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi.

Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic."

"Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos."

Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system.

Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms.

AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS

Elon Musk presents a $1 million check during an America PAC town hall ahead of the Wisconsin Supreme Court election, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on March 30, 2025. (Jamie Kelter Davis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," said Glavin.

"When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle."

In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin.

"This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that."

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," one expert said. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success.

One of the most obvious recent examples is former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate.

Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections.

"Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them."

JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026

Michael Bloomberg discusses his presidential run on Nov. 25, 2019, in Norfolk, Virginia. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)

John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes.

According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact.

Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he said could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage.

"Most people understand that new technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he said. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world."

He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front.

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added.

Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent."

"It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving.

THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES

Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin addresses party members at the DNC's summer meeting, on Aug. 25, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News)

One source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C.

While Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion.

Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns."

He also said voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government."

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS

The massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving, one expert said. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

"I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, said, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway.

Seeberger echoed Arlinghaus’ claim that Republicans may have squandered some of their financial advantage by making poor spending decisions, saying, "When you're spending the majority of those sums to talk about issues that register low on the rankings of what voters say are their priorities, there's going to be limited returns on the impact."

#6040. Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”

President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

Trump also wrote that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

Various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also announced on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the company’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

We also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the company is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

And we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

Huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his company to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of the investigations’ conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

It's that time of year again: Your last chance to plan your final flights or mattress runs of 2026 in order to snag last-minute elite status for next year.

If you hold Marriott Bonvoy elite status and aren't going to requalify for your status tier this year, there's good news: The program is extending its “soft landing” policy into 2027. With this policy, if you fail to requalify for your current status this year, you will only drop one tier from March 2027 until February 2028.

Related: Marriott elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Based on the program's elite-status policies, the Marriott Bonvoy status you earned in 2025 will expire at the end of February 2027 unless you requalify for your current level or higher in 2026. But what if you don't meet the threshold for the same or higher status?

That's where Marriott's generous soft landing policy comes in. Whether you qualify for a level far below your current status or don't qualify for status at all in 2026, you'll only drop one status tier in 2027.

According to Marriott's website, members who don't requalify for status will see their new, lower tier take effect in early March 2027, and they can enjoy this status through February 2028. Meanwhile, if you requalify for your existing tier or a higher tier, you will also hold this status through February 2028.

This soft landing policy, which Marriott has offered for years, is a win-win: It provides valuable benefits to elite members who weren't able to requalify for status, while giving them a reason to stay loyal to Marriott and perhaps try again for status next year.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Marriott Bonvoy elite status offers some excellent perks, such as room upgrades, late checkout and even lounge access. Thankfully, with this soft landing policy, mid- and upper-tier elite members who don’t requalify this year won’t be left empty-handed. You can still enjoy the benefits of the next-lower tier from March 2027 to February 2028.

For example, with Titanium Elite status, expiring Ambassador Elite members will enjoy many of the same perks of their current status, including complimentary breakfast at most brands, suite upgrades at check-in, 75% bonus points earned on stays and a status match to United MileagePlus Premier Silver status.

You should see your new Marriott status and updated expiration in early March.

#6038. Newsom shredded for ‘hypocritical’ claim Trump 'sells' pardons after moving to spare 548 death row inmates

California Gov. Gavin Newsom defends his plan to commute 548 death sentences to life without parole and accuses President Donald Trump of using pardons to reward allies. Credit: Office of California Gov. Gavin Newsom

California Gov. Gavin Newsom's calls for federal reforms to presidential pardon powers are garnering intense backlash for "hypocrisy" after he used his state-level executive powers to spare hundreds of death row inmates from receiving the death penalty.

Trump vowed Monday to direct the Justice Department (DOJ) to seek the death penalty for child murderers and speed up federal executions after Newsom’s announcement.

Online fury erupted after Newsom posted a video defending his decision to commute the death sentences of 548 criminals while accusing President Donald Trump of turning "the power of mercy into a business."

"Gavin, is the arsonist calling for a ban on fire," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted on X. "Man who commuted 548 death row sentences is now deeply concerned about abuse of the pardon power."

NEWSOM ORDERS CALIFORNIA’S MOST REVILED KILLERS OFF DEATH ROW – 10 OF THE WORST WHO COULD BENEFIT

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is facing backlash on social media after calling for federal reforms to President Donald Trump's pardon powers despite Newsom's plan to spare 548 death row inmates from receiving the death penalty. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu via Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

One X user noted how Trump "just told the DOJ to fast-track the death penalty for child killers and predators. [Gavin Newsom], on the other hand, is proudly defending his decision to spare 548 of the worst of the worst.

Another user posted, "Are you f---ing kidding me? His arrogance and hypocrisy are immeasurable."

"After pardoning everyone on death row in California, Newsom calls for reform of the president’s pardon powers," another wrote on X. "You can’t make this stuff up."

Trump called out Newsom at the DOJ alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and family members of victims of the 548 death row inmates. He referred to the inmates as "the most evil monsters on the face of the Earth," and accused Newsom of stealing closure for the victims' families.

Some of the crimes committed by inmates who will no longer face the death sentence include slaughtering entire families, torturing and murdering children and killing police officers.

In Newsom’s video, he defended his decision to commute the death sentences to life without parole, accusing Trump of abusing his pardon powers.

"Donald Trump doesn’t oppose mercy. He sells it," Newsom said in the video. "If you’re poor, Black or Brown, you get the needle. If you’re rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."

SLAIN FIREFIGHTER'S MOTHER PLEADS WITH TRUMP TO INTERVENE AFTER NEWSOM STOPS KILLER'S DEATH SENTENCE

Trump issued 220 total pardons in his second term as president and 143 during his first term. While Trump has granted pardons to wealthy individuals and political allies, he has also pardoned Black Americans, most notably Alice Marie Johnson, who was serving a life sentence for drug trafficking and money laundering offenses before he commuted her sentence in 2018 and pardoned her in 2020.

Trump has been criticized for his comments Tuesday that a pardon for Jensen Huang was "always an option" ahead of the Nvidia CEO's scheduled appearances before Congress next week following his re-instatement after claims he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vice President JD Vance told reporters Wednesday when asked about the potential.

Part of the blowback against Newsom also stems from his decision to override California voters' rejection to abolish the death penalty, defending his clemency authority as an example of "when law as applied cannot be squared with justice."

"And the Governor of CA should not be able to sell out crime victims and prosecutors by overriding juries, judges and the WILL of CA voters," a former Sacramento District Attorney posted to X. "Worst Governor in history."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said Monday he led 14 attorneys general in condemning Newsom’s plan, arguing Newsom had overridden juries, courts and California voters.

Some critics have speculated Newsom's move to revoke California inmates death sentences is a tactic gearing up for his bid as the Democratic nominee for the 2028 presidential election. He is seen as one of the top candidates for the party.

JAMES CARVILLE WARNS GAVIN NEWSOM FACES CALIFORNIA BAGGAGE IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN

Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks March 26, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Frazer Harrison/WireImage)

"You should think twice about this decision," a user said. "You may personally end up needing a Presidential pardon one day."

A coalition of California prosecutors and victims’ relatives asked the state Supreme Court last week to halt Newsom’s plan, arguing that he failed to give families a chance to be heard before pursuing the commutations. Newsom asked the justices to act before his term ends in January.

California voters rejected measures to abolish the death penalty in 2012 and 2016. The state last carried out an execution in 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019.

Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr and Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

#6036. DOJ lawyers ordered to swarm 'frivolous' 97,000-lawsuit wave from ICE detainees

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.

Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful.

Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday calling on attorneys working outside of immigration issues to assist in the lawsuits described by Blanche as "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security."

The pre-Thanksgiving memo comes as the Justice Department has been hit with 97, 000 habeas corpus petition filings since January 2025, including close to 10,000 new petitions filed since October. Typically, the Justice Department faces only a few hundred habeas corpus cases a year.

As President Donald Trump has made mass deportations a centerpiece of his second administration, with Department of Homeland Security figures showing nearly 1.2 million illegal immigrants removed to date, the Justice Department has seen a wave of petitions.

DHS TOUTS HIGHEST ICE DEPORTATIONS IN HISTORY, AS MULLIN SAYS AGENCY HAS BEEN ‘UNLEASHED’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detain dozens of immigrants inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in New York City on June 26 after their court appearances, amid a surge in federal court challenges from detained migrants. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The surge in lawsuits comes after the Trump administration changed its detention policy to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the U.S. — even those who have lived in the country for years. Without access to bond hearings before immigration judges, detainees have turned directly to federal district courts to challenge their confinement.

In a post on X sharing the memo, Blanche accused judges who have granted detained immigrants' habeas corpus petitions of being "corrupt" and seeking to "release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation."

"Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Blanche wrote. "That is why it is imperative that all Department attorneys who litigate civil matters support prosecutors who have shouldered the burden of habeas petitions for nearly two years."

SUPREME COURT TO SCRUTINIZE KEY PILLAR OF TRUMP DEPORTATION MACHINE IN BLOCKBUSTER CASE

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing for his nomination to be attorney general at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, DC, on July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Blanche's memo calls on attorneys from four civil litigation divisions — Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources — as well as the U.S. Trustees Program and senior leadership offices, including those of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general, to assist. Within the next 30 days, leadership from the respective divisions must submit an "aggressive appellate strategy" for tackling the habeas corpus claims and deploy attorneys to high-volume districts. The memo does not explicitly state how many of the department's roughly 2,000 civil litigators will be utilized.

Blanche acknowledged that divisions are already carrying "a significant workload in light of personnel reduction."

TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN COULD STRENGTHEN ADMIN'S HAND IN LOOMING SUPREME COURT FIGHT

A corridor inside the immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building in New York on May 20, as the Justice Department mobilizes civil litigators to fight tens of thousands of habeas corpus petitions from detained migrants. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I also know that many attorneys have already volunteered or offered support in litigating habeas matters," Blanche wrote. "By ensuring that attorneys are assigned no more habeas matters than each attorney can adequately and zealously defend, combined with providing jurisdiction-specific resources, I hope to mitigate any significant disruption to attorneys' current dockets."

Blanche's memo drew criticism from immigration attorneys, including Reza Mazaheri, who called the attorney general's characterization of judges as "corrupt" "slander."

"If I walk into a courtroom and accuse a judge I disagree with of corruption, I would undoubtedly face disciplinary action," Mazaheri wrote on X. "In the public service sphere, the word 'corruption' has a distinct meaning."

Meanwhile, Bridget Pranzatelli, a staff attorney at the National Immigration Project, told Newsweek that the influx of habeas corpus petitions is the result of a change in how the Trump administration interprets bond hearing statutes.

"Many of them would have gotten a bond hearing before this administration suddenly changed its interpretation of a decades-old law to fill beds that private prison companies get paid for," Pranzatelli said in a statement.

The memo comes as the U.S. Supreme Court prepares to hear arguments in early 2027 in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, a high-stakes challenge to the administration's mandatory detention policy. In October, the justices agreed to review a second U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling that struck down ICE's policy of denying bond hearings to illegal immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for years. The court's decision — expected by late June or early July 2027 — will resolve a split among federal appeals courts and determine the fate of tens of thousands of pending habeas petitions.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

#6035. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

Wyndham Rewards recently revised its fixed award chart, expanding from three to four redemption tiers.

The 15,000- and 30,000-point tiers remain, while free nights now start at 5,000 points instead of 7,500. Wyndham also added a 45,000-point tier for a select number of its highest-tier hotels and redistributed thousands of properties across all four tiers.

The new top tier is 50% higher than the former 30,000-point maximum, a devaluation in anyone's book. However, the new astonishingly low 5,000-point tier was what caught my attention. What exactly do you get for so few Wyndham Rewards points?

As someone who can't resist a great deal, I checked into one of these hotels to find out whether it was an amazing new sweet spot or a night I would rather forget.

Related: Wyndham Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more

On a recent visit to Kansas and Missouri, I checked the Wyndham Rewards website and saw that the area had several properties for just 5,000 points per night.

I chose the Super 8 by Wyndham Riverside/Kansas City, mainly for its proximity to the beautiful new Kansas City International Airport (MCI). The next morning, I was flying to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) before continuing to Europe in a lie-flat seat for less than the price of a cup of coffee.

At the time of booking, the hotel had a 2.8-out-of-5 score based on 84 ratings on Wyndham's website, which did not fill me with confidence. However, the Wyndham Rewards member rate for my night was $96.21 including taxes and fees. Redeeming 5,000 points therefore gave me 1.92 cents per Wyndham point, about 3.5 times TPG's November 2026 valuation of 0.55 cents per Wyndham point.

Related: It’s easy to earn Wyndham Diamond status — here’s how and why you should care

I took a Lyft from downtown Kansas City, Missouri, to Riverside, a small suburb on the north bank of the Missouri River. First impressions of the property were that it was pretty remote, with nothing really nearby other than the Argosy Casino.

There was plenty of parking, and the 48 rooms were spread across a two-story motor-inn-style building.

While the property was less than 20 years old and was renovated in 2010, the rather garish lime-green lobby looked ready for another refresh.

I was quickly helped by a very friendly attendant, who I believe was the franchisee, and his wife, who also greeted me warmly.

There were several property rules listed on the counter with normal restrictions on smoking and pets in rooms.

What raised an eyebrow was the rule that visitors were allowed in guest rooms for only 60 minutes maximum, which made me wonder what kind of visitors might be passing through the doors and for what purpose in one-hour blocks.

The attendant thanked me for being a Wyndham Rewards member and quickly handed me my room key. So far, the experience had been better than the 2.8-out-of-5 rating suggested, but the room would be the biggest test.

I nervously opened the door to find a comfortable room with a king-size bed, plenty of pillows, a large flat-screen TV, a minifridge and a workspace.

Like the lobby, I doubt this decor will win any design awards, but it was clean, quiet and comfortable, and everything worked.

The separate bathroom had a tub/shower combo and a spotless toilet with several towels for me to choose from.

If I had one complaint about the room, it was that the showerhead was pulling away from the bathroom wall, but it still provided a steady flow of hot water.

The property was light on other amenities: There was no fitness center, swimming pool, bar or restaurant. However, the Argosy Casino was a few minutes' walk away, so there was plenty to keep me occupied for the evening.

After a good night's uninterrupted sleep, all guests even received a complimentary breakfast, with toast, cereals, juice and coffee available.

This is a great deal for a 5,000 point redemption with no resort fee.

Related: How I earned 24,500 points from $180 in hotel stays

The staff bid me a friendly farewell when I checked out, and I was on my way to the airport after a comfortable, peaceful and stress-free stay.

Wyndham Rewards are easy to earn, as they transfer at a 1:1 rate from the following transferable rewards:

But the best transfer option is for anyone with Wells Fargo Rewards points. This is because rather than transferring at a 1:1 rate, they transfer at a much more generous 1:2 rate. This means you would only need 2,500 Wells Fargo points to book a 5,000-point Wyndham Rewards hotel night, and Wells Fargo points can be transferred in any increments, unlike the strict 1,000-point increments of most transferable rewards.

Given that Wyndham Rewards properties offering 5,000-point nights regularly sell these nights for around $100 cash, this is an easy way to get around 4 cents per Wells Fargo point, more than twice TPG's valuation of Wells Fargo Rewards points.

Barclays also offers four Wyndham Rewards branded credit cards. Depending on the card and, in some cases, when it was opened, eligible cardholders receive a 10%, 20%, or 25% discount on free-night redemptions. That reduces a standard 5,000-point night to 4,500, 4,000 or 3,750 points, respectively.

Wyndham's new 5,000-point redemptions will not put you in a luxury hotel, but this stay was terrific value for money and delivered a clean, quiet room, a comfortable bed and a simple breakfast before an early flight.

The decor was dated, and the loose showerhead fixture needed attention. Even so, the friendly service and uninterrupted night's sleep were far better than the hotel's 2.8-out-of-5 rating had led me to expect. For a one-night stay near an airport, I would give it 4 out of 5.

Redeeming 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points instead of paying the nearly $100 member rate will give you 2 cents' worth per point. Even better, a traveler transferring from Wells Fargo Rewards would need just 2,500 points for the same award — I can't think of a more valuable way to use Wells Fargo points.

I would happily stay at a property like this again for just 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points per night.

More than 50 House lawmakers, led by Rep. Darrell Issa, are raising alarms over what they call discriminatory South Korean policies that harm American tech companies and tilt economic advantages toward China-linked competitors.

FIRST ON FOX — The White House accused South Korea of breaking a promise to President Donald Trump to treat U.S. tech companies fairly, telling Fox News Digital that Seoul has since hit Coupang with hundreds of millions of dollars in fines.

South Korean regulators have hit Coupang with roughly $688 million in fines, including a provisional $224 million penalty against its food delivery service, which was announced this month.

A White House official said the administration opposes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's alleged discrimination against U.S. companies and that the White House expects South Korea to keep its commitment to fair treatment for U.S. technology companies, including Coupang.

EXPLOSIVE HOUSE REPORT REVEALS SECRET OPERATION INSIDE CHINA AT CENTER OF SOUTH KOREA'S FIGHT WITH US COMPANY

President Donald Trump welcomes South Korean President Lee Jae Myung at the White House in Washington, D.C., Aug. 25, 2025. (Brian Snyder/Reuters)

A South Korean embassy official punched back at the White House's allegation that there was a direct targeting of Coupang, stating that the nation abides by the agreement with the Trump administration and is committed to a fair and nondiscriminatory business environment.

"All investigations and decisions undertaken by the Korean government, including the recent fine imposed on food delivery service providers for anticompetitive conduct by the Korean Fair Trade Commission have been conducted lawfully and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations," a spokesperson for the Embassy of the Republic of Korea told Fox News Digital. "Furthermore, the right to seek legal remedies under the Korean law is fully guaranteed."

The spokesperson explained that South Korea considers its strategic partnership with the U.S. its most important relationship, describing an alliance built on democracy, the rule of law and open markets, adding that Seoul will keep working closely with American policymakers to correct the record and deepen economic ties between the two countries.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung at the Gyeongju National Museum in Gyeongju, South Korea, Oct. 29, 2025. (AP)

Although nearly all its business is in South Korea, Coupang is an American company. It is incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Seattle and listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company was founded in 2010 by Korean American entrepreneur Bom Kim, who dropped out of Harvard Business School.

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, center left, and his wife, Kim Hea Kyung, arrive to depart for China at the Seoul airport in Seongnam, South Korea, Jan. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/Lee Jin-man)

Yoon Suk Yeol, of the People Power Party, was elected president in 2022 but was impeached in December 2024, largely for his attempt to declare martial law.

The Democratic Party is South Korea's main liberal party and favors progressive domestic policies. The country's conservatives have historically favored less engagement with North Korea and stronger ties with the U.S.

The company said it drove more than $5 billion in overseas sales of American goods and services in 2025.

The Coupang Inc. logo atop the company's headquarters, in Seoul, South Korea, on Dec. 15, 2025. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., during a House Judiciary Committee field hearing in New York, on April 17, 2023. (Stephanie Keith/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"For eight decades, America and Korea have benefited from an alliance purchased by sacrifice on the battlefield, joined by economic opportunity, and bolstered by mutual values," Issa told Fox News Digital. "But that is being put at risk by the anticompetitive policies of KFTC Chairman Ju that have unfairly targeted America’s tech industry and even individual American citizens," he added.

In July, the House Judiciary Committee outlined a timeline of the South Korean government's scrutiny of Coupang, from a secret laptop recovery mission in China directed by South Korea's National Intelligence Service to the agency's request that the National Assembly pursue perjury charges against Harold Rogers, interim CEO of Coupang Corp., the company's South Korean subsidiary.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, center, waves the national flag and cheers during the 80th anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule in Seoul, Aug. 15, 2025. (AP)

#6031. House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

“My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

“I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”

It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., said everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

#6027. Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

“When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

“We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

“When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

“Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

Flight cancellations quickly climbed on Thanksgiving Day as a coastal storm put a damper on holiday travel — and festivities — up and down the East Coast.

Heavy rain and wind fueled flight cancellations at several of the nation's busiest hubs. And the flight woes were at risk to worsen as the storm system tracked north.

By mid-morning on Thursday, Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) had seen the most significant impact. More than a quarter of the day's flights at the airport had been shuttered as of 9:30 a.m. EST, according to FlightAware.

Those cancellations dealt a blow to operations at Southwest Airlines, the dominant carrier at BWI, which led all U.S. airlines with 125 cancellations Thursday.

Travel disruptions had also begun to mount at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and LaGuardia Airport (LGA), which had collectively seen dozens of flights scrapped.

The culprit: the same foul weather that led to the postponement of the nearby Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

This week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' plans.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself is typically one of the quietest days of the year at airports.

Forecasters had projected the remnants of the storm could cause lasting delays into Friday, before it peters out by Saturday.

All eyes will be on how Mother Nature cooperates on Saturday and Sunday, as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

Here are some things you should do if you're planning to fly in the next few days.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.
