Fox News Digital spoke to Defending Education senior communications director Erika Sanzi about Pritzker’s decision to opt out of a Trump administration tax credit funding Illinois student scholarships through a federal school-choice initiative.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes.

Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative.

In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics.

GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION

"At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote.

"We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics."

Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states.

Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions.

"It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz said in a press release.

"Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states."

Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids."

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS

Students raising hands while teacher asking them questions in classroom. (iStock)

Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — New York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets.

The U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead."

Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name."

"May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added.

Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state.

A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi said about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program.

"You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he said in relation to his decision."

Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment.

The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight."

Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#6023. Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a plan from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

“I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen said. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”

The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a new suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move quickly.

Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

At the earlier appearance, Daines said that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

“We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

But Democrats have been debating whether to use their new majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

Democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

Schumer has said he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

“I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the big things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen said.

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

#6019. GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”

Democrats said Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

Democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

“First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”

Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

“We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”

Ueland said his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”

For example, he said GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland said he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, said he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” said Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, said by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”

He said GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”

The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

The right travel credit card is important for any trip, as it can earn points or miles and provide valuable travel protections. But when you travel for months at a time, other factors — including no foreign transaction fees, international acceptance and benefits you can use outside the U.S. — become especially important.

Living and working on the road without a permanent home base puts these priorities to the test. The best card benefits solve practical problems and remain useful long after a typical vacation would have ended.

With that in mind, these are some of the best cards for long-term travelers and digital nomads.

Now, let's dive into what each of these cards has to offer.

All of the welcome bonus valuations in this guide are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

The is best for long-term travelers who want broad travel protections, premium lounge access and flexible points in one card.

Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is an excellent card for long-term travelers because it earns at least 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining purchases.

The card's up-to-$300 annual travel credit is straightforward to use, while Chase Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access can provide a place to work, eat and recharge between flights. The card also charges no foreign transaction fees.

Its travel protections are another reason why it's a great choice for digital nomads. Baggage delay coverage, for example, can help cover essentials when your checked bag doesn't arrive on time. Trip delay and trip cancellation/interruption coverage can also soften the financial hit when plans unravel.

Plus, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to hotel and airline partners, including fan favorites like United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt.

However, the card carries a $795 annual fee, and several of its statement credits are tied to particular merchants.

Cardholders can get up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year for qualifying prepaid stays of at least two nights through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, with a maximum of $250 per transaction. It can be a fantastic perk when a long trip calls for a comfortable hotel reset between apartment stays or after a long-haul flight.

If you spend most of the year outside the U.S., weigh the $795 annual fee against the benefits you’ll use regularly.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The is best for digital nomads who can use its extensive lounge network, hotel elite status and premium perks.

The Amex Platinum comes offers one of the largest airport lounge networks available. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes access to Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required for Priority Pass Select).

That pairs nicely with a high earning rate on flights booked directly with the airline as well as up to a $200 airline fee statement credit every calendar year on your selected qualifying airline (enrollment required; terms apply).

Cardmembers can transfer their Membership Rewards points to Amex's airline and hotel partners, opening up award flights and hotel stays worldwide.

Several other card benefits lend themselves nicely to travelers who stay in hotels, rather than long-term rentals. Hotel elite status, including Hilton Honors Gold Elite, Leaders Club Sterling and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite, can make your stays more comfortable (enrollment required).

The up-to-$600 annual lodging statement credit adds more value to the card and can give you an excuse to add luxe stays to your itinerary. It is split into two up to $300 semiannual credits and applies to qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe, Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®. (Airbnb Luxe and THC require a minimum two-night stay; FHR will also require a minimum two-night stay beginning Jan. 1, 2027; terms apply).

It's worth noting that you likely won't be able to use every statement credit. Someone spending a lot of time outside the U.S. may have trouble using several U.S.-focused perks, including Uber Cash (for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders) and Walmart+.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

The Venture X is best for digital nomads who want premium travel perks and simple rewards on everyday spending.

For digital nomads, the Venture X works well because of how little strategy it requires, at home or abroad. It earns 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases outside bonus categories. These flat-rate, hassle-free rewards are useful when your spending habits change from one country to the next.

The card allows you to transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel partners. That's even more flexibility when your travels take you all over the world.

The card's $300 annual Capital One travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth $100 toward bookings made through the Capital One Travel portal) are very easy ways to offset the annual fee.

Primary cardholders also receive complimentary access to Capital One Lounges, Capital One Landings and participating Priority Pass lounges.

The card offers cellphone protection when you pay your monthly wireless bill with it (up to $800 per eligible claim, with a $50 deductible and a maximum of two claims per 12-month period). That's useful when your phone is your boarding pass, map and connection to work.

The offers a useful middle ground for digital nomads who want strong everyday rewards without paying a hefty annual fee.

At $95 a year, the Strata Premier is the easiest card on this list to justify. Its protections are particularly practical when you live out of a suitcase. The card's 24-month extended warranty can be especially useful when living on the road, as nomadic life can take a toll on electronics and other gear.

Cardholders can transfer ThankYou points to more than 20 airline and hotel partners. There's also an annual $100 hotel benefit per calendar year for a single hotel stay (of $500 or more; excluding taxes and fees) booked through CitiTravel.com or by calling Citi. That's a fast way to offset the card's $95 annual fee.

The Strata Premier offers fewer statement credits than pricier cards. Its $95 annual fee makes it a good fit if you’re traveling on a budget or want an affordable second card.

The is best for everyday spending abroad, thanks to its earning rate on eligible foreign transactions.

For digital nomads, the card's value comes from a benefit that applies well beyond Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights. Cardholders earn 3 Atmos Rewards points per dollar spent on foreign transactions, whether that's a hotel stay, meal, pharmacy visit or souvenir.

You'll also get a 10% rewards bonus on points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

Atmos Rewards points can be redeemed for flights on Oneworld carriers and other airline partners, in addition to Alaska and Hawaiian.

The annual Global Companion Award provides a 25,000-point discount when two travelers book award travel on the same itinerary. Based on our valuations, this benefit alone is worth $400. That's enough to justify the annual fee, even if you never touch the other Alaska or Hawaiian-specific benefits.

Cardholders who spend $60,000 in a card anniversary year can earn an additional Global Companion Award worth up to 100,000 points. Since these awards can be used in any class of service, the larger award could be particularly valuable for a premium-cabin or long-haul partner redemption.

That same $60,000 in spending earns 30,000 status points. Combined with the 10,000 status points awarded after each account anniversary, you'd have enough for Atmos Gold status (mapped to Oneworld Sapphire). On eligible itineraries, that's good for business-class lounge access — even when you're flying economy — priority check-in and boarding, preferred seating and extra baggage.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Summit card.

Many long-term travelers and digital nomads run businesses from the road. These travelers may find it useful to have one or more business cards as well.

One business card that's particularly well-suited to this lifestyle is the (see rates and fees).

This card earns 3 points per dollar spent on travel, shipping, social media and search engine advertising, and cable, internet and phone services (on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The Ink Business Preferred also offers cellphone insurance, primary rental car insurance on business-related rentals and no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

When you live out of a suitcase, the best card benefits aren't always flashy. What matters is what follows you: protections when your laptop dies or your flight gets canceled, solid rewards on everyday spending in any currency and lounges in the airports you actually pass through.

A long list of statement credits might only be great if you'll be back home in a few days. For extended travel, it's more important to pick the card that works wherever you wake up tomorrow.

#6016. For ‘Denuclearization,’ Trump Should Build Up to Build Down

The president ought to take a page from Reagan’s Cold War playbook.

The U.S. Navy Ohio-class ballistic missile submarine USS Tennessee returns to Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay, Ga., in 2013.

Mass Communication Specialist First Class James Kimber/U.S. Navy/Handout via Reuters

President Trump left his Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin last week still dreaming of a denuclearization agreement with his great-power counterparts. But Trump’s long-held ambition to achieve the deep reductions in nuclear weaponry that Ronald Reagan secured with his Soviet counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s clashes with reality. Chinese and Russian officials may now be speaking the language of “strategic stability,” but Trump would be wise to recognize that these pronouncements are intended to deter him from taking the steps necessary to strengthen America’s nuclear deterrence.

Unlike Gorbachev in the final years of the Cold War, neither Xi nor Putin currently has any appetite for meaningful arms-control negotiations. Xi acts as if his geopolitical position compares favorably with America’s. Both men are wielding their nuclear power to weaken America’s security and dissolve its alliances. Consider Putin’s nuclear threats during the war in Ukraine and Xi’s campaign of coercion in the western Pacific, which is shielded by China’s growing nuclear arsenal.

Kyle Balzer is a resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute where he specializes in nuclear strategy and policy.

#6014. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

From left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

Democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

"This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

Ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

Wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

The Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

The bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, plan and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member New Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as currently drafted.

However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an issue: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the new Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

Merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

Some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

"I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley said before the vote Thursday night.

But Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental issues under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

After decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

Lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

#6013. Chris Van Hollen’s Anti-Israel Turn

The Maryland senator has become an unlikely opponent of the Jewish state — and that’s boosted his fortunes in the Democratic Party.

Senator Chris Van Hollen (D., Md.) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C, November 19, 2026.

It’s a well-established gambit. A politician starts criticizing Jews. He gains followers. His attacks grow, along with his political power.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen (D.), who is challenging Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate majority leader, is adopting this playbook. Van Hollen, who alleged in a recent New York Times op-ed that Israelis have “increasingly undermined American interests and values,” has become one of the foremost critics of the Jewish state in Congress. Backed by progressives such as Bernie Sanders, he is basking in his newfound fame. His foray into the Senate leadership contest coincided with his push to strip provisions concerning U.S. security cooperation with Israel from the National Defense Authorization Act. These and other broadsides have made him a darling of the anti-Zionist left. Regardless of whether he supplants Schumer, Van Hollen is pushing the Senate ever leftward on its policy toward Israel.

Senator Chris Van Hollen (D., Md.) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C, November 19, 2026.

Daniel J. Samet is a Jeane Kirkpatrick Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. He interned for then-Representative Van Hollen in 2015.

#6012. Wanted: A Strategy Chief to Bring Air India’s Two Airlines Closer

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Air India's new custom designed B787-9. Air India

IndiGo hired Air India Express' former chief as its strategy officer in March. Now Air India is creating a strategy role of its own. It looks like both airlines agree the job is worth having.

Air India is creating a new group strategy officer position as part of its efforts to get full-service carrier Air India and its low-cost arm Air India Express working together more closely, sources said.

Rival IndiGo made a similar move earlier this year, naming former Air India Express managing director and CEO Aloke Singh as its chief strategy officer. Singh ran Air India Express for five years before joining IndiGo.

The new strategy job is one of two group-level roles being added. The other is a chief of the training academy, who will be responsible for bringing the group’s flying academy, flight training organizations and technical training under one roof.

Air India CEO and managing director Tewolde Gebremariam outlined the changes at an employee town hall on Wednesday. He also spoke about operational improvements, cost cutting, network changes and the airline's longer-term plans.

Air India is adding two group-level roles — a group strategy officer and a head of its training academy — as part of a push to run Air India and its low-cost arm Air India Express as "One Air India Group," sources said. CEO and Managing Director Tewolde Gebremariam outlined the changes at an employee town hall on Wednesday. Both carriers keep their own air operator certificates and customer-facing, operational, and regulatory work, while finance, HR, IT, and centers of excellence move to group level to cut duplication and bring costs closer to rivals. The airline is also reworking its hubs in response to regional airspace restrictions: more westbound connecting traffic through Mumbai, more eastbound connections through Delhi, with Bengaluru under consideration as a third hub. Air India has estimated the Pakistan airspace closure takes about $455 million a year off profit before tax, Skift reported. Gebremariam said on-time performance has improved over the past three months and that October and November were encouraging, with revenue per available seat kilometer increasing, but he described profitability as the harder problem with fuel costs high. A cost transformation program led by senior executives has collected more than 1,500 employee suggestions for saving money.

#6011. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Your Questions Answered

Questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12

The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on new Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

Premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen said “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

The front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

Skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

With jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

Premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921

Premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium plan 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

Two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135

Two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card company that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

The clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody shows the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

American is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

The premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12

The evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

Unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

ZS’s Kunal Shah said the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

Premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

No contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758

American announced the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air New Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

The real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

The industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12

Chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

The local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

New York is where the gap between the big three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting shows three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

American’s disclosed JFK plans are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside new Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

United has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

American’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its New York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

Delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the new Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO said this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

Skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK plan as route and product-level on the current record.

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

Apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The company posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer said the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

The structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

Treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

Points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21

The pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

The open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

For airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23

The shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under new silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

The profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

No cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1

U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12

Where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and said explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

The lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

Nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Big Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he says he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15

This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He said chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

JetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

The parts of JetBlue’s current plan that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

One caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a new entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

The delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13

The squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

Breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 showed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

Neeleman said Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

The commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

Scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Big Four skip.

Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

Neeleman said majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

The practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman said the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

The second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

Reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman said helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the company’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

Breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has said directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13

Breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into big cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and said chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

Breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman plans a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its new routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321

Scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The issue is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

The catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 announced changes since early 2025 1.

The unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper said consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45

Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

— Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.
